description: Oxidation, reduction, the reactivity series, acid reactions, pH scale and making salts.
content_html:
Oxidation and Reduction

Oxidation is the gain of oxygen or the loss of electrons. Reduction is the loss of oxygen or the gain of electrons. These two processes always happen simultaneously in redox reactions. A useful mnemonic is OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss (of electrons), Reduction Is Gain (of electrons).

For example, when copper oxide is reduced by carbon: \(2CuO + C \rightarrow 2Cu + CO_2\). The copper oxide loses oxygen (it is reduced); the carbon gains oxygen (it is oxidised). The carbon is the reducing agent and copper oxide is the oxidising agent.

Key Fact

In a redox reaction, the oxidising agent causes the oxidation of another substance but is itself reduced. The reducing agent causes the reduction of another substance but is itself oxidised. This is a common source of confusion — always track both substances separately.

At Higher Tier you must also explain redox in terms of electron transfer. In the reaction between magnesium and oxygen: \(Mg \rightarrow Mg^{2+} + 2e^-\) (magnesium is oxidised — it loses electrons); \(O_2 + 4e^- \rightarrow 2O^{2-}\) (oxygen is reduced — it gains electrons). The substance that loses electrons is the reducing agent; the substance that gains electrons is the oxidising agent.

The Reactivity Series

The reactivity series lists metals in order of their tendency to react — specifically, how readily each metal is oxidised (loses electrons). Metals above hydrogen in the series can displace hydrogen from dilute acids. Metals higher in the series can displace metals lower in the series from their salt solutions — these are called displacement reactions.

The order of metals in the reactivity series can be remembered using a mnemonic. From most reactive to least reactive, the series runs: potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, zinc, iron, tin, lead, hydrogen, copper, silver, gold, platinum. Metals above hydrogen react with dilute acids to produce hydrogen gas. Metals below hydrogen (copper, silver, gold) do not react with dilute acids. This knowledge allows chemists to predict whether a given displacement reaction is possible: if a more reactive metal is added to a salt solution of a less reactive metal, a displacement will occur. If the added metal is less reactive than the metal in solution, no reaction takes place.

When zinc is added to copper sulfate solution: \(Zn + CuSO_4 \rightarrow ZnSO_4 + Cu\). Zinc is more reactive than copper, so it displaces copper from the solution. Zinc is oxidised (loses electrons, forms \(Zn^{2+}\)) and copper ions are reduced (gain electrons, form Cu atoms). The blue colour of the copper sulfate solution fades as colourless zinc sulfate forms, and a reddish copper deposit appears. This is both a displacement reaction and a redox reaction.

Acids, Alkalis and the pH Scale

The pH scale runs from 0 to 14. A pH below 7 indicates an acidic solution (high concentration of \(H^+\) ions); pH 7 is neutral; above 7 is alkaline (high concentration of \(OH^-\) ions). Strong acids (such as hydrochloric acid, HCl) fully dissociate in water into ions, whereas weak acids (such as ethanoic acid) only partially dissociate. It is important to distinguish between a strong acid (degree of ionisation) and a concentrated acid (amount of acid dissolved per litre) — a concentrated weak acid is not the same as a strong acid.

Key Fact

Strong acid: fully dissociates into ions in water (e.g. HCl \(\rightarrow H^+ + Cl^-\)). Weak acid: partially dissociates (e.g. ethanoic acid). Concentrated: many moles of acid per litre. Dilute: few moles per litre. These are independent properties — a strong acid can be dilute.

Neutralisation and Making Salts

Neutralisation occurs when an acid reacts with a base or alkali. The general equation is: acid + base → salt + water. For example, hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide: \(HCl + NaOH \rightarrow NaCl + H_2O\). At the ionic level, the \(H^+\) ion from the acid reacts with the \(OH^-\) ion from the alkali: \(H^+ + OH^- \rightarrow H_2O\).

Acids also react with metals, carbonates and metal oxides. Key reactions to know:

  • Acid + metal → salt + hydrogen (e.g. \(Zn + H_2SO_4 \rightarrow ZnSO_4 + H_2\))
  • Acid + metal carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide (e.g. \(CaCO_3 + 2HCl \rightarrow CaCl_2 + H_2O + CO_2\))
  • Acid + metal oxide → salt + water (e.g. \(CuO + H_2SO_4 \rightarrow CuSO_4 + H_2O\))

In your practical work (PAG C2), you will carry out acid-alkali titrations to find the volume of acid needed to exactly neutralise a given volume of alkali. A suitable indicator (e.g. methyl orange or phenolphthalein) is added to the alkali in a conical flask. Acid is added from a burette drop by drop until the indicator changes colour permanently at the end point. The titration is repeated without indicator to produce a pure salt solution, which can be evaporated carefully to obtain crystals. Concordant results (within 0.10 cm³ of each other) are used to calculate the mean titre.
exam_tip_html: A common error in 3-mark Explain questions on redox is confusing the oxidising agent with the substance that gets oxidised. Remember: the oxidising agent is the one that gets reduced (it oxidises something else). For questions on acids, do not use ‘strong’ and ‘concentrated’ interchangeably — examiners penalise this substitution. In salt-preparation questions, name the acid correctly: HCl makes chloride salts, H&sub2;SO&sub4; makes sulfate salts, HNO&sub3; makes nitrate salts.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Oxidation is the gain of oxygen or loss of electrons; reduction is the loss of oxygen or gain of electrons. OIL RIG is the key mnemonic. The oxidising agent is itself reduced; the reducing agent is itself oxidised.
  • The reactivity series orders metals by reactivity. More reactive metals displace less reactive metals from salt solutions — these are redox reactions. Strong acids fully dissociate in water; weak acids partially dissociate. ‘Strong’ and ‘concentrated’ are not synonyms.
  • Neutralisation: acid + base → salt + water. Key reactions: acid + metal → salt + hydrogen; acid + carbonate → salt + water + CO&sub2;; acid + metal oxide → salt + water. The salt formed depends on the acid used.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly defines oxidation?
A) Gain of electrons or loss of oxygen
B) Loss of electrons or gain of oxygen
C) Gain of electrons or gain of oxygen
D) Loss of electrons or loss of oxygen
practice_questions.marks: B) Loss of electrons or gain of oxygen [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the products formed when zinc reacts with hydrochloric acid.
practice_questions.marks: Zinc chloride (ZnCl₂) and hydrogen (H₂). [1 mark — both required]

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between a strong acid and a concentrated acid.
practice_questions.marks: A strong acid fully dissociates (ionises) into ions in water [1 mark]; a concentrated acid has a large amount (many moles) of acid dissolved per unit volume, regardless of how strongly it ionises [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: When magnesium is added to copper sulfate solution, a displacement reaction occurs. Explain why this reaction is also a redox reaction, identifying which species is oxidised and which is reduced.
practice_questions.marks: Magnesium is more reactive than copper (higher in the reactivity series), so it displaces copper [1 mark]; magnesium is oxidised (it loses electrons / forms Mg²⁺ ions) [1 mark]; copper ions are reduced (they gain electrons / form Cu atoms) [1 mark].

practice_questions.text:
A student wants to make copper sulfate crystals by reacting copper oxide with sulfuric acid.

Write a word equation for this reaction and describe how the student would obtain pure crystals of copper sulfate from the resulting solution.
practice_questions.marks: Word equation: copper oxide + sulfuric acid → copper sulfate + water [1 mark]; add excess copper oxide to warm sulfuric acid and stir until no more dissolves [1 mark]; filter to remove excess copper oxide [1 mark]; evaporate the filtrate slowly / heat gently to concentrate then allow to cool and crystallise [1 mark].

practice_questions.text:
Explain what happens during a neutralisation reaction between an acid and an alkali. In your answer, include:
• the ionic equation for the reaction
• why neutralisation is considered a redox reaction or not
• how you could use titration to produce a pure salt solution.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Correct ionic equation (H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O) with explanation that acid provides H⁺ ions and alkali provides OH⁻ ions; clear statement that neutralisation is NOT a redox reaction (no electron transfer, no change in oxidation state); detailed titration procedure including indicator, burette, end point detection, and repeat without indicator to obtain a pure solution; evaporation to produce crystals.
Secure: Correct ionic equation; neutralisation correctly identified as not redox with justification; titration procedure mostly correct.
Developing: Ionic equation present or partially correct; some titration steps described; redox point attempted.
Emerging: Basic statement that acid + alkali = salt + water; limited detail on titration or ionic equation.

knowledge_checks.q: What happens to the oxidising agent in a redox reaction?
options: It is oxidised and loses electrons
It is reduced and gains electrons
It is neither oxidised nor reduced
It loses oxygen and gains electrons

flashcard_questions.q: What does OIL RIG stand for?
flashcard_questions.a: Oxidation Is Loss (of electrons), Reduction Is Gain (of electrons).

flashcard_questions.q: In a redox reaction, what happens to the oxidising agent?
flashcard_questions.a: It is reduced — it gains electrons (or loses oxygen).

flashcard_questions.q: In a redox reaction, what happens to the reducing agent?
flashcard_questions.a: It is oxidised — it loses electrons (or gains oxygen).
A list of metals in order of their reactivity, from most reactive to least reactive.
A strong acid fully dissociates into ions in water.
A concentrated acid has many moles of acid dissolved per litre of solution.

flashcard_questions.q: What are the products of: acid + metal carbonate?
What is the ionic equation for neutralisation?
What salt is produced when hydrochloric acid reacts with sodium hydroxide?
What happens to the pH of a solution as more acid is added to an alkali?
In the displacement reaction of zinc with copper sulfate, which species is oxidised?
flashcard_questions.a: Zinc — it loses electrons and forms Zn²⁺ ions.

glossary_terms.definition: A reaction where a substance gains oxygen or loses electrons.
A reaction where a substance loses oxygen or gains electrons.
A substance that donates electrons or removes oxygen from another substance, causing the other substance to be reduced. The reducing agent itself is oxidised.
A substance that accepts electrons or provides oxygen to another substance, causing the other substance to be oxidised. The oxidising agent itself is reduced.
A list of metals in order of their reactivity, from most reactive (potassium) to least reactive (gold).
A scale from 0 to 14 that measures the concentration of hydrogen ions in a solution; below 7 is acidic, 7 is neutral, above 7 is alkaline.
The reaction between an acid and an alkali (or base) to produce a salt and water.
